entries.title: A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades
entries.summary: El Niño rains have transformed Chile's Atacama Desert into a spectacular sea of color, awakening a fleeting ecosystem of flowers and wildlife in one of the driest places on Earth.
entries.content:
A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades

COPIAPÓ, Chile — A vast swathe of Chile's Atacama Desert is now a patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples stretching across the craggy desert floor as far as the eye can see.

This winter, heavy rains brought by the El Niño super cycle caused flash floods in the Atacama Desert, with some areas receiving the heaviest rainfall since records began in the 1950s.

Floodwaters in July and August destroyed or damaged dozens of homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate.

But the floral bloom that followed has been the largest and most colorful in 30 years — and perhaps ever.

The rainwater penetrated deeper into the parched ground than it has in decades, allowing millions of seeds, bulbs and tubers to sprout above the surface. Many had lain dormant for decades under the sand.

More than 200 species are in flower. A month ago, the first plants to emerge created a pale-yellow haze. This was followed by a soft purple hue as other bulbs germinated. Now, almost every indentation and crevice in the desert is streaked with color.

Scientists studying the phenomenon say there are patches of desert in bloom where flowers have never previously been recorded, suggesting that bulbs have remained dormant there since before the phenomenon was first studied in detail in 1997.

"This is a natural seed bank, a dormant archive that becomes a living one with the rains," says Moisés Grimberg, the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park.

"But it's a race against time — this brief biological window allows these species to complete their life cycle, which lasts roughly two to three months."

Llanos de Challe is a 113,000-acre national park along the arid coastline, where waves lap at pristine white sand beaches.

Grimberg says the park normally receives about 10,000 visitors a year. But with the desert in bloom, 15,000 tourists have visited over the last few weeks alone.

Across the desert, the roads are lined with tourists' cars. According to Chile's national tourism board, the region is expected to see around 300,000 overnight trips during the two months the desert is in bloom.

Among the star attractions are the nectar-filled, crimson flowers of the garra de león, with their long tails of flame-like green leaves. This endemic flower is coaxed out of dormancy by the rains and grows along just a few miles of this stretch of coastline in the Atacama Desert — nowhere else in the world.

This bloom occurs every few years in what is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth. But scientists say the phenomenon is becoming more frequent as changes in the climate bring unseasonal rains.

The phenomenon gives rise to a thriving, transient ecosystem, with insects hatching and attracting lizards and bats, as well as larger mammals such as the guanaco.

Biologists from INIA, Chile's national seed bank, are collecting specimens to analyze in their laboratory before the brief flowering season ends.

"It's very exciting," said Ana Sandoval as she delicately shook seeds free from their casings to take back to INIA's taxonomist at its base in northern Chile.

"It's as if the desert is awakening. Sometimes people think it's an empty, arid place, devoid of life, but actually our desert is just waiting for the right conditions, and any precipitation, to awaken it."

The seed bank wants to preserve the genetic material and unique adaptations each plant has developed to survive the extreme, arid conditions.

Sandoval points out different ways plants harvest water as she walks. Some leaves are covered in fine hairs; others have a thick waxy cuticle.

A national park dedicated to the desert bloom was created in June 2023 to protect a 141,000-acre area where flowers spring up every few years. Now local authorities want to go further.

Miguel Vargas, the governor of the Atacama region, is beginning the process of seeking UNESCO World Heritage recognition for the desert bloom phenomenon.

"This represents a tremendous opportunity to strengthen special interest tourism and diversify our regional economy, which is currently heavily reliant on mining," he said. "Receiving UNESCO recognition would put the Atacama region on the world stage."

Vargas hopes this will become Chile's eighth World Heritage site within a couple of years.

This year, the bloom is projected to last until mid-November.

As the flowers begin to fade, scientists will be left with two tantalising questions: was this the Atacama Desert's largest flowering event on record, and might closer examination reveal any previously unknown species among the millions of plants?

entries.title: Climate change is altering the colors we see in the world: an illustrated journey
entries.summary: From Arctic landscapes to insect bodies, climate change is shifting the familiar colors of nature.

entries.title: In Maine, a new approach to practicing medicine in the sky
entries.summary: Air medical service comes with high risks, high costs, and staffing struggles. To reduce turnover and serve rural patients, LifeFlight of Maine is putting the needs of healthcare workers first.
entries.content:
In Maine, a new approach to practicing medicine in the sky

Clipboard in hand, pilot Will Bradbury stands near a helicopter at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. He's running down emergency landing tips with his crew.

"If we need to get out quickly because of smoke or fire, just watch the terrain so that you're not walking uphill into the rotors," he reminds flight nurse Denise Saucier and paramedic Brian Merklin.

The team is getting ready to take off on a medical transport flight. Saucier folds herself into the compact helicopter. She's worked for the air ambulance service for seven years and still calls it a dream job.

Dream job or not, the life of a flight clinician is hard and, given the headwinds slamming rural healthcare, getting harder.

Since 2015, demand for medical flights in Maine has doubled. In 2025, LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights, more than one every three hours. This year, demand is up another 10%.

Nationwide, air medical services are filling the gaps left behind as rural hospitals close, convert to outpatient-only rural emergency hospitals, or stop offering unprofitable services like labor and delivery.

And, as Medicaid cuts estimated by the Congressional Budget Office at $911 billion over ten years take effect, it's going to get worse. Hundreds more rural hospitals or maternity departments are at immediate risk of closing. With every closure, medical care gets further away.

And, increasingly, ground ambulance stations, many of which are also struggling to keep their doors open, can't meet the need. That leaves flight clinicians like Saucier and Merklin seeing more patients every day.

"We're seeing this across the board. The need for air medical services is increasing year over year," says Nicholas George. He runs the ETHOS Database, a national tracking system for air medical programs.

When the rural health care system breaks, EMS — on the ground and, increasingly, in the air — is the backstop.

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

Healthcare of last resort

Every week or two, Saucier finds herself on a flight to one of Maine's thousands of islands. Occasionally, crews even land in the state's vast forests and mountains, then take snowmobiles to reach patients.

But "scene calls" to roadside — or trailside — accidents are less than 10% of LifeFlight's transports. (They're a higher percentage in urban areas.)

Most are interfacility transports, like today's. They'll stabilize a patient at a small, local hospital and fly them to a larger, better resourced one.

Saucier glances out the window for hazards. The view still reminds her of the role the organization plays in Maine, one of the country's most rural states.

"You go so long of a distance without seeing any houses, any roads," Saucier says. "It really hits home how rural Maine is and how necessary EMS is in the state."

And the pressure is on air ambulances as ground services in Maine are increasingly strained. The system is so fragmented that patients can fall through the cracks. Last year, a woman in a small northern Maine town died while the county dispatch center called 10 ambulance services. None responded.

Air ambulance services, though, come with unique challenges, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. It's been difficult to retain staff with the medical expertise to treat everything from heart attacks to injuries to fragile newborns, and who can stick with the demanding job without burning out.

Almost a quarter of ground-based EMS workers leaves the field every year. While there's no comprehensive staffing data for air medical services, flight clinicians face a slew of unique stresses, including dangerous conditions; long shifts and unpredictable hours; ever-increasing training and certification requirements; and significant mental health burdens. And then there's the pay, which is low throughout emergency medical services.

For years, LifeFlight retained only 60% to 70% of its workers, says CEO Joe Kellner.

"This is a really hard job," Kellner says. "By their job description, they are seeing people on their worst day, over and over again."

Training elite clinicians

This year, for the first time in nine years, LifeFlight is nearly fully staffed. One of the nation's handful of independent nonprofit air medical companies, LifeFlight has taken an innovative approach to the problems that plague the industry, including a combination of better training, higher pay and in-house mental health support.

Mike Abernethy, an EMS expert and retired emergency medicine professor at the University of Wisconsin, considers the company one of a handful of model programs for the industry. LifeFlight of Maine is a nonprofit, unlike much of the industry, which is dominated by for-profit businesses with reputations for charging exorbitant prices.

"There's just absolutely no comparison in the aviation and medical quality of these programs" versus an average for-profit air medical business, Abernethy argues.

When Kellner, a paramedic himself, became CEO in 2023, he began addressing the recruitment and retention problems. What LifeFlight calls the "Critical Care Academy," a six- to eight-month orientation program, is intended to address both issues.

Emergency critical care advances quickly. So most clinicians need regular education, both to remain successful on the job and to get hired in the first place.

On another day at headquarters, four instructors sit in a claustrophobic control room. Through a window looking into what appears to be a hospital room, paramedics Daniel Horne and Brad Alleger are undergoing an annual skills assessment, a simulation of a real-life medical crisis.

Dr. Dave Saquet turns on a mic and coughs. "It's hard to breathe," he whispers urgently. "It hurts everywhere."

His voice seems to be coming from the patient — a breathing, bleeding mannequin lying on a hospital bed.

"What happened to you?" Horne asks.

"My house was on fire," Saquet chokes out.

A wall monitor displays the patient's vital signs — which Saquet is manipulating on his laptop.

Medics and nurses here do simulations often, both to pass the Critical Care Academy, and also to stay up to date on occasional but critical events, like emergency births, newborn resuscitation, and burns. Before the assessment ends, the paramedics will have tried and failed to intubate the patient. After that "failure," they performed an emergency procedure to enable breathing, switching from the mannequin to a pig trachea.

Because it's hard to find recruits qualified enough for the rigorous training, the company also started a mentorship program for people considering applying. Some even attend the academy, gaining skills even if they'll never work for LifeFlight.

Success comes slowly: Recently, LifeFlight hired one of last year's mentees.

Experiments

Kellner instituted an unusual change that he says even nurses endorse: LifeFlight raised paramedics' pay to match flight nurses' compensation. Industrywide, paramedics make less. That keeps costs down, which is why pay equity is rare. Kellner believes the change has helped with recruitment.

Another experiment: LifeFlight hired a full-time mental-health counselor.

EMS workers' rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety and depression are more thanfive times higher than the average American's.

"That has led people to leave this profession," Kellner says.

That was true for paramedic Brian Merklin, who was working for a different service in Nevada during the pandemic.

"We got hit really hard," he says. "The crews were just flying nonstop. We did four-day shifts, so for 96 hours we were just going, going, going."

About a third of the staff quit, he says. "They were getting air medical service plus COVID, right in the teeth."

Eventually, Merklin too needed a break. He left the profession for a few years. Then, when he felt the urge to fly again, he found LifeFlight.

Today's trip

The helicopter, which took off from Bangor, lands on a community hospital's rooftop helipad. Merklin and Saucier hurry to the patient's side. Most LifeFlight patients are unconscious or too ill to consent to share their stories, so the details are private. The injuries are shocking. If this patient doesn't get to a trauma center quickly, they might die.

Merklin and Saucier are unfazed.

But it's this kind of incessant trauma exposure that makes mental health support for first responders so invaluable.

Merklin serves on a peer support team.

"There's a lot of lip service paid … to the cost to your mental health in this profession. But this is the only place I have ever worked that actually provided support," he says. "I would love to see it take hold in other areas."

If counseling keeps two or three people from leaving, it's a wise investment, Kellner argues: "The cost of training somebody new into our organization is about $100,000."

As both air and ground EMS become even more essential, the task is to recruit and keep more people like Merklin and Saucier.

Because, if hundreds more hospitals do close, highly trained EMS workers may be the only people standing between patients dying and getting the care they need.

Elaine Appleton Grant's reporting was supported by the National Institute for Health Care Management.

entries.title: How Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave for Democrats
entries.summary: Republicans made gains with young voters in 2024, but in this year's midterms Americans under 30 issued a strong rebuke of President Trump and his party, voting decisively for Democrats instead.
entries.content:
How Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave for Democrats

Democrats have done well in recent elections when they win young voters by a margin of at least 20 points. On Tuesday, they carried Gen Z — those under 30 — by nearly 50 points, according to exit polling.

It's a stunning shift from 2024, when the party lost critical ground with young people. Long seen as a part of the Democratic base, voters under 30 shifted right towards Donald Trump, motivated by his pledge to better their economic prospects.

But this week, the youngest generation of voters issued a strong rebuke of Republicans, taking another chance on Democrats and their change-focused message at a moment when many of them feel as though the American Dream is out of reach.

How young voters powered Democrats to victory

Americans ages 18-29 have a history of turning out at lower rates than older voters, and this year was no exception. Gen Z made up 11% of the total vote on Tuesday.

However, where young Americans may have made the greatest difference, is on the margins in House and Senate races where Democrats flipped seats.

The Texas Senate race is a key example. Democrat James Talarico won the state by 12 percentage points, however, when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.

Loading...

Explaining the massive shift from 2024

When assessing gains more broadly, Democrats argue the party's strong slate of candidates helped drum up increased enthusiasm.

But another motivating factor remains strong opposition to Trump. Throughout his second term, Gen Z increasingly soured on the president, with some arguing he failed to make good on a number of core campaign promises — from pledging to lower prices and repeatedly vowing "no new wars," to calling for a crackdown on federal corruption and the release of the Epstein files.

Loading...

Much of that disappointment was reflected in exit polling. Economic issues were the top concern for a plurality of 18-29 year olds, at 43%, and these voters expressed broad frustrations with Trump's handling of the issue. More than eight in 10 said that Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions, with similar shares opposing his tariff strategy and the decision to go to war with Iran.

The young voters Trump lost

Early analysis from CIRCLE indicates that 15% of young people who backed Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate in this year's midterms.

Democrats made gains with some young voters that backed Trump two years ago, including white men and Latino men, two blocs that narrowly voted Republican in 2024 and then voted blue on Tuesday by double digits. Democratic candidates also narrowed the margins with young rural voters and people without college degrees.

Some of those gains may have been helped by young Trump voters who chose to sit this election out, but it's unclear how many of them there were.

How the election results broke down by age

Loading...

The midterm results underscore how neither of the two major parties owns Gen Z, according to John Della Volpe, a left-leaning pollster who's extensively studied the politics of young Americans.

"The cohort of younger people in this cycle had a different set of experiences than the cohort of people two years ago, or four years before that," he said. "Every candidate, every party has to earn their votes."

Della Volpe, who runs the Harvard Youth Poll, notes that in the latest survey, released in October, there was a sizable enthusiasm gap between young Democrat and young Republican respondents. While half of Democrats said they definitely planned to vote, just a third of Republicans and less than a quarter of Independents said the same.

"I also think we shouldn't over read what's happened," he added. "Clearly a significant historic rebuke on the party in office — that's obvious — however, I think we need to more fully, kind of understand, the contour of the electorate, who showed up and who didn't show up."

By 2028, Gen Z and millennial voters will make up more than half of the electorate, a demographic shift with huge implications for Democrats and the GOP.

"Young adults can make a difference," said Elizabeth Matto, who serves as the director of the Center for Youth Political Participation at Rutgers University.

"They do care about politics. They can sway the outcome of elections. And they're a voting bloc worth paying attention to."

entries.title: UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary
entries.summary: President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White.
entries.content:
UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.

Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson.

White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump's post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.

When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, "Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already."

He declined to say what conversations he'd had with Trump but said, "I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."

Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump's post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words "On to the next chapter."

The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.

Trump said in his post that he requested that White bring along several UFC fighters as "assistants," adding, "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!"

While White didn't make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States, he did elsewhere in his news conference describe his ambitions to expand the Zuffa Boxing organization he also runs with Saudi Arabian backers and hold more of its events around the world.

Trump's post came as his White House is in a period of major transition and struggling with his party's deep losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president's impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump's inner circle.

The shake-up at the heart of his administration follows the brief but tumultuous week when Trump tried out a new press secretary in Katie Zacharia, who seemed uncomfortable in her sole appearance before reporters before leaving the job after five days.

The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August. Trump remains without a chief spokesperson.

Trump is close friends with White and has attended several UFC events with him since returning to the White House in January 2025.

He brought White and the sport to the White House's South Lawn in June for the celebration of America's 250th year of its independence and the president's own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed near the executive mansion under " The Claw," a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.

"It was an amazing experience, this was a one-of-one," said White afterward.

White also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

entries.title: Homelessness in the U.S. saw its largest drop in more than a decade last year
entries.summary: Homelessness declined after years of record-high levels but it still remains at nearly 700,000. The Trump administration and homeless advocacy groups cite different reasons for the drop.
entries.content:
Homelessness in the U.S. saw its largest drop in more than a decade last year

After years of increasing to record-high levels, the homeless population in the U.S. dropped more than 6% in 2025. That amounts to roughly 49,000 fewer people without housing. It's the second year in a row that homelessness has declined, with a smaller drop in 2024.

"President Trump's actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness," Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner said in a press release announcing the results of an annual count in communities around the country. The agency had not yet posted a detailed report.

A second independent analysis based on the same count, but commissioned by the advocacy group National Alliance to End Homelessness, found a similar decline but credited different reasons for it.

"It's good news that more people are getting housed, and that the programs that are funded by Congress are working," said CEO Ann Oliva.

Both analyses find there's still nearly 700,000 people in the U.S. living in shelters or on the streets, significantly more than before the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Trump administration cited its changes in immigration policy as a key factor in the decline. During the Biden administration, New York, Chicago, Boston and Denver all saw a surge in asylum seekers who turned up at homeless shelters. "That's also the four cities that have driven half of the drop most recently," said Devon Kurtz, Public Safety Policy Director at the Cicero Institute, an administration ally on homelessness policy.

Kurtz also pointed to declines in cities like San Francisco, which is moving to support more sober-living options, housing that bans drugs and alcohol. But critics say that can send more people back to the street if they relapse, which is common.

The Trump administration argues that the requirement to be drug-free would help more people achieve recovery, and wants to expand such programs. In fact, the administration wants to overhaul several billion dollars in homelessness spending and shift it toward short-term housing with mandated addiction and mental health treatment. So far that's been blocked by courts.

The administration says longstanding federal policy of getting people into permanent housing first, then offering voluntary treatment, has failed, and is to blame for the pandemic spike in homelessness. But Oliva, with the homelessness alliance, said programs that get people off the street without preconditions were a big part of the latest declines, especially among veterans.

"Investments in programs like that are much closer to the scale of need for veterans than for any other population experiencing homelessness," she said. Homelessness among U.S. veterans was down more than 7% last year, and has declined nearly 60% since 2010.

By contrast, Oliva said more permanent housing is needed for people who are chronically homeless, and more likely to suffer from mental health problems and addiction. Unlike other groups that saw a decline last year, there was a small uptick in people who've been homeless for a long time.

HUD also credited a crackdown on homeless encampments after the Supreme Court in 2024 said cities can ban people from sleeping and camping in public places. Oliva said the analysis her group commissioned showed that cities with such bans "actually did worse than the national average."

Oliva noted last year's decline in homelessness was broad and likely due to a number of factors, including softening rental markets in some places. Even though rents are still high they're down from record peaks during the pandemic, and that could stem the flow of newly unhoused people.

There were also declines in places that saw major weather disasters, like western North Carolina and Hawaii. When HUD and other groups move in to help those displaced, unhoused people also get assistance they did not have before.

entries.title: The surprising and often forgotten history of economic populism in Texas
entries.summary: NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with Austin-based political commentator David Griscom. He authored a book titled The Myth of Red Texas which tells the story of economic populism in Texas.
entries.content:
The surprising and often forgotten history of economic populism in Texas

NPR's Rob Schmitz speaks with Austin-based political commentator David Griscom. He authored a book titled The Myth of Red Texas which tells the story of economic populism in Texas.

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

As the votes came in on election night Tuesday, some of the most shocking results were in Texas. The blue wave did not stop at the border of the Lone Star State. Democrats swept the top races in Texas with James Talarico winning a Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa winning the race for governor.

Austin-based political commentator David Griscom was perhaps not as surprised to see his state flip. Earlier this year, he published a book titled "The Myth Of Red Texas: Cowboys, Populism, And Class War In The Radical South." He joins us now. Welcome.

DAVID GRISCOM: Thank you so much for having me. It's been a really wonderful past few days.

SCHMITZ: What great timing, with a book title like that. Texas, obviously, as you've written, has a reputation for being a reliably red state, but as we've seen, it's a lot more complicated than that. How did Texas Democrats pull this off?

GRISCOM: Well, I think in a lot of ways, you saw Texas Democrats returning to our roots here. You know, many people forget this, but Texas was once the hotbed of kind of left-wing, pro-working-class politics. Going all the way back to the 1890s, we were the heart of the populist movement, and it's no accident that James Talarico, Clayton Tucker and Gina Hinojosa all call themselves populists.

Using this kind of rhetoric, I think, really focuses on the billionaires and the folks who are harming our democracy. And I think that gave a lot of people who might have been waiting for an excuse to maybe buck the Republican Party, which has dominated state politics here for so long, the opportunity to do so.

SCHMITZ: Let's go back in history a little. You know, Texas politics are often associated, you know, with oil billionaires, conservative evangelical voters and the Republican establishment. You know, your book, "The Myth Of Red Texas," tells the story of, you know, working-class, populist tradition that oftentimes goes overlooked. Tell us a little bit about that.

GRISCOM: So there's multiple phases of this. It's an entire kind of generation or tradition in Texas politics that has been forgotten. My book opens up talking about barbed wire, which we all associate with Texas. But when barbed wire first comes to Texas, it was fiercely resisted. There was an episode called The Fence Cutting War, and this happened all across the state, where working-class cowboys got together and they started cutting down these new barbed wire fences because they saw these as a tool that was being used to dispossess them.

This then flows into the populist movement, which was born right here in Texas in Lampasas, where a bunch of farmers got together and they started asking themselves why those who work most get least and those who work least get most. And they started to look around and realize that it was the monopoly powers, the power of the banks, and it was the corruption of the politicians.

SCHMITZ: I want to dig in a little bit on that and the populism aspect of this. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has embraced the populist label with open arms. You know, I want to play a clip here from an interview that she did before the election with The New York Times.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

GINA HINOJOSA: Populism is about economic power. We see that things are so stacked against working people in this country. Fighting culture wars at this time is not a winnable fight, and that is not the fight of 2026.

SCHMITZ: And that's really interesting. I mean, she's separating her and Talarico's style of politics from Democrats elsewhere, who have sort of engaged more in identity politics. Is there something uniquely Texan about Hinojosa's or Talarico's approach as Democrats?

GRISCOM: Absolutely. So again, you know, Texas has had major swings before where everyday working people - cotton farmers, Black and white - they were able to unite working people, the vast majority of people, on messages about the ways that they can improve their life. And that's what Gina and James were able to do. They didn't run a partisan message, and that is a long tradition that has existed in this state.

I'd also add, if I could, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez - after 2024, she made a very strong point about how effective some of the anti-trans ads that the Trump administration put out were - you know, they are for they/them, Trump is for you. And AOC said, like, this was a problem with Democrats. When a lot of people were feeling economic pain, they felt that the things that Democrats were interested in weren't immediately important to their lives.

And in this election, the table was kind of reversed because all of the ads in Texas were about anti-LGBTQ things, anti-trans. And when somebody's talking about that - in this case being Republicans - when you're really struggling to get by, it does really show that these folks are out of touch with your economic needs, and that really helped Gina and James, for sure.

SCHMITZ: That is David Griscom, author of "The Myth Of Red Texas." David, thank you.

GRISCOM: Thank you so much.

entries.title: Oklahoma tribes say proposed legal changes put ancestral lands in Ohio at risk
entries.summary: The Trump administration has proposed changes to the National Historic Preservation Act that could endanger historic sites significant to tribal nations across the country. Oklahoma tribes say that puts ancestral lands in Ohio at risk.
entries.content:
Oklahoma tribes say proposed legal changes put ancestral lands in Ohio at risk

Oklahoma tribes says proposed legal changes puts ancestral lands in Ohio at risk

The Trump administration has proposed changes to the National Historic Preservation Act that could endanger historic sites significant to tribal nations across the country. Oklahoma tribes say that puts ancestral lands in Ohio at risk.

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

Tribal leaders in Oklahoma whose ancestral lands are across the country in Ohio say sacred sites are under threat. Changes favored by the Trump administration to the National Historic Preservation Act could weaken much needed protections, they say. Reporters at member stations WYSO and KOSU take us to both places.

ADRIANA MARTINEZ-SMILEY, BYLINE: I'm Adriana Martinez-Smiley in Ohio, which is home to hundreds of earthworks sacred to Native Americans, like the Miamisburg Mound, one of the largest conical mounds in the eastern United States, rising 65 feet.

MICHELLE COLLINS: Once you get up there, you can just sit and kind of take in a view, a really fantastic view, of the Miami Valley.

MARTINEZ-SMILEY: Miamisburg Mayor Michelle Collins calls the structure awesome.

COLLINS: You're talking something that's a couple thousand years old.

MARTINEZ-SMILEY: The mound was built by the Indigenous Adena Culture. The National Historic Preservation Act, which has been around for 60 years, protects sites like this. Section 106 of the Act allows states, tribes or local governments to consult with federal agencies on development proposals and redesign projects to mitigate harm to sites.

However, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, a federal agency, and Congress are separately proposing changes. Their revisions would narrow what's considered damaging to a site and make consultation optional. Democratic Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico says the current rules also cause too much of a delay when it comes to approving energy projects.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MARTIN HEINRICH: America needs to be able to build things in years, not in decades.

MARTINEZ-SMILEY: Advocates say the proposed changes should streamline the permitting process. However, tribal officials say the changes could undermine the responsibility the federal government has to cooperate with tribal nations.

SARAH LIESE, BYLINE: I'm Sarah Liese in Oklahoma. There are 38 federally recognized tribal nations in the state. For some, Ohio was once their home, but they were forcibly displaced to Oklahoma due to broken treaties and federal policies in the 18th and 19th centuries. Chief Ben Barnes of the Shawnee Tribe says the National Historic Preservation Act should remain as is.

BEN BARNES: The Section 106 consultation process allows the Shawnee Tribe and other tribes to make sure that sacred sites, such as the earthworks in Ohio or ancestral burial grounds or places of sacred memory, are preserved.

LIESE: Barnes says they also want to protect the spaces where they currently live, and it's key that Native Americans still have a say in the process with no optional provision about their involvement.

BARNES: We have a very large gas line that runs across Oklahoma to Springfield, Missouri. And one day, that gas line is going to need to be disturbed or going to need to be enlarged or need to be repaired. And without having Section 106 processes, they can do that without ever consulting the people that gather in that place to worship.

LIESE: Blake Norton, an official with the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, says these sites are much more to them than places needing development. He likens it to stripping away the humanity of his ancestors and disregarding the relationship Native Americans have to these spaces.

BLAKE NORTON: And for what? So a project can be completed? So that capitalism can continue?

LIESE: In a statement, Senator Heinrich says he's speaking with tribal leaders about possible compromises on the bill. For NPR News, I'm Sarah Liese in Oklahoma.

MARTINEZ-SMILEY: And I'm Adriana Martinez-Smiley in Ohio.

entries.title: Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government
entries.summary: Gadi Eisenkot ran as the main rival to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but neither won enough support to command a majority. Israel's main parties have recommended Eisenkot form a new government.
entries.content:
Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government

Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, to try to form the next government. It's a setback for Netanyahu, whose party won the most seats but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.

Netanyahu's Likud party won 27 seats in last month's election, six more than Eisenkot's Yashar party. But neither secured enough support to command a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament.

President Isaac Herzog will formally give Eisenkot the mandate at 5 p.m. local time on Sunday. Herzog made the decision after parties representing most of the members of Israel's parliament recommended Eisenkot to try forming a governing coalition.

Eisenkot is a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, serving as the country's top military commander from 2015 to 2019. A veteran of several military campaigns, he later joined Netanyahu's emergency war cabinet following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel, but left the following year, accusing Netanyahu of failing to make progress toward ending the Gaza war and securing the release of hostages.

Eisenkot lost his son, Gal, a reservist killed in Gaza, as well as two nephews during the war.

He leads the center-right Yashar party, which he founded on an anti-corruption and government reform platform. He will now have 28 days to put together a coalition government, with a possible 14-day extension.

That gives him up to six weeks to negotiate with rival parties and secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.

The coalition building promises to be a tough task and could include strange bedfellows: from ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to Arab-led parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel — who make up about 20% of Israel and had a record turnout in these elections.

They could now potentially be the kingmakers. But both Eisenkot and Netanyahu ruled out working with them before the elections. Now there's some public pressure on Eisenkot to change his mind, and on Saturday Netanyahu issued a video warning against that.

He said it would be partnering with what he called Hamas supporters and "those who oppose Judaism." Eisenkot responded, calling Netanyahu's video hysterical.

If Eisenkot fails, Herzog can give another lawmaker a chance to form a government. If those efforts also fail, Israel could face another election. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister in the meantime.

entries.title: Polish gunman who killed 6 people in Krakow has 'ultranationalistic' views, authorities say
entries.summary: A gunman targeted random people as he drove into Krakow's Main Square, a major tourist spot. Police shot and wounded the gunman during a gunfight.
entries.content:
Polish gunman who killed 6 people in Krakow has 'ultranationalistic' views, authorities say

KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — A Polish man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow on Saturday and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 15 others before police shot and wounded him, authorities said.

The attack, which Poland's defense minister described as an "act of terror," happened in Main Square, which is in the heart of Krakow's Old Town and is a major tourist hub in the country's second-largest city.

The 25-year-old attacker drove to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each stop with an automatic weapon, authorities said. Although they didn't release his name, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the man holds "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Hours after the attack, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities found the bodies of three of the suspect's close family members — two women and a man — inside of his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow.

"We have the next acts of this tragedy," Tusk told reporters.

Four women and two men were killed in the Krakow attack. At least three of the women were Polish, and one of the dead was a U.K. citizen, authorities said. Police were still trying to identify the other two people who were killed.

A total of 13 people were hospitalized in serious condition, authorities said, though that figure may include the gunman, who underwent surgery after the attack.

It's unclear how many of the injured were shot. Two of them were treated and released within hours of the mass shooting. Two police officers were seriously injured, Kierwiński said. Five non-Poles were also injured, police commander Marek Boroń said.

People were wounded at several locations

The attacker wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, and used a military-type long gun, Krakow police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said. Police found other weapons and ammunition in his car. He kept firing at the police even after being shot himself, she said.

The attacker engaged in a "wild ride" around Main Square, which is why people were wounded at several locations, said Cisło, adding that the gunman appears to have acted alone.

Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city will be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Krakow will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy.

"The square will belong to us again," Gibała said in a video posted on X.

Mass shootings are rare in Poland

Videos posted on social media by witnesses show people running away from the square to take cover on small streets nearby, as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims. In one video, a police officer is seen repeatedly shooting the attacker, who is lying on the street, only to later slowly collapse himself to the ground.

Photos showed a Polish Medical Air Rescue helicopter after it landed in the square.

It wasn't immediately clear whether the gun used in the attack or those found in the attacker's car are legal. Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising.

Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children.

The Krakow attacker's military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other "extreme right lone actors" committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague. "We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland."

Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski announced increased security measures, including road barriers, along main streets in the old town in the Polish capital in the aftermath of the Krakow attack.
